newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian building society merger seen forerunner.
newsitem.headline: Australian building society merger seen forerunner.

text.p: The creation of a new building society giant via a three-way amalgamation of leading players in the Australian state of Queensland has paved the way for further rationalisation in the state's non-bank financial sector.

"We see further rationalisation as other societies follow our methodology," Neil Axelby, chairman of First Provincial Building Society Ltd, one of the merger parties, said in an interview on Thursday.
First Provincial, Australia's oldest continuously operating building society, is 120 years old this month.

Earlier on Thursday, First Provincial and Northern Building Society Ltd announced they planned a merger with Sunstate Credit Union to create the state's biggest building society with estimated assets of more than A$1.1 billion.

Northern's chairman Brian Roebig, who is to become chairman of the renamed First Australian Building Society, told Reuters he thought the enlarged size of the new entity was still not big enough to attract a takeover move from any of the major banks.
"I don't think so. For the larger banks, we are still too small," Roebig said.
"What it does do is make other building societies think about their own future," he said.

He also pointed to the difficulties of a takeover bid given the complicated voting structure of building societies which allowed one holder-one vote rather than a one share-one vote system in commercially listed companies.
Axelby said cost savings of A$5 million annually would come from three main areas - information technology merging, branch rationalisation and reduced staff levels, mainly through natural attrition.

With the nearest bank competitor, the Bank of Queensland Ltd, still with an asset base twice First Australian's size, competition was seen in the ranks of friendly societies and the non-bank mortgage providers, Roebig said.
Axelby agreed with market analyst estimations that First Australian would have a combined lending book of about A$750 million.
New consumer targets would include enlarged commercial lending, particularly to small business, he said.
"We see mainly small business products in this area, not large corporates," Axelby said.
Roebig also indicated a move into telephone banking services to help to minimise cost structures.
Listing of the new entity would be most likely maintained by First Provincial adopting a name change to First Australian, Axelby said.
The merger deal was subject to regulatory approvals from the Australian Financial Institutions Commision (AFIC), and due diligence, to be completed by August 22.
Shares in the only listed participant in the proposed merger, First Provincial, jumped 25 cents, or 10 percent, to close at A$2.75 on Thursday.
